Course description

Vibrations and waves are everywhere. If you take any system and disturb it from a stable equilibrium, the resultant motion will be waves and vibrations. Think of a guitar string—pluck the string, and it vibrates. The sound waves generated make their way to our ears, and we hear the string’s sound. Our eyes see what’s happening because they receive the electromagnetic waves of the light reflected from the guitar string, so that we can recognize the beautiful sinusoidal waves on the string. In fact, without vibrations and waves, we could not recognize the universe around us at all!

The amazing thing is that we can describe many fascinating phenomena arising from very different physical systems with mathematics. This course will provide you with the concepts and mathematical tools necessary to understand and explain a broad range of vibrations and waves. You will learn that waves come from many interconnected (coupled) objects when they are vibrating together. We will discuss many of these phenomena, along with related topics, including mechanical vibrations and waves, sound waves, electromagnetic waves, optics, and gravitational waves.

Exercise:
TITLE: Practice Final Exam 1

8.03SC Physics III: Vibrations and Waves
Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Fall 2016
Practice Final Exam 1 (covers Lectures 1-23)


Problem 3.1 (16 pts)

The electric field for a TE mode in an infinitely long (in the x direction) perfectly conducting rectangular waveguide (a < b) is given by

    E⃗(x,y,z,t) = E₀ cos(k_y y + φ_y) cos(k_x x − ωt) ẑ

[Figure 1: A perfectly conducting waveguide — a rectangular box drawn in perspective with its long axis along x, extending indefinitely to the right (the open end is drawn with dotted lines and a wavy field pattern inside). The y-axis points up and the z-axis points toward the viewer, both from the origin at the near-left corner. The height of the box along y is labelled a, and the depth along z is labelled b, with a < b. The guide is infinitely long in the x direction.]

(a) Find k_y and φ_y that satisfy the boundary conditions.
(b) Write down the dispersion relation for this mode of the waveguide.
(c) What is the lowest frequency that will propagate in this mode?
(d) What is the magnetic field B⃗(x,y,z,t) associated with the electric field of this mode?


Problem 3.2 (16 pts)

The figure below shows a system of masses. The mass of 2m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant 2k, while the mass of m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant k. The masses are then coupled to each other with an elastic band of length L, under tension T = 2kL. The masses are constrained to move in the x direction only. At equilibrium the masses have the same x position and the springs are uncompressed. There is no friction or gravity. The displacements from equilibrium are small enough (x₁, x₂ ≪ L), so that the tension in the band stays constant.

[Figure 2: A system of coupled oscillators — two vertical walls, one on the left and one on the right, with the region between them drawn in a vertical plane. Axes at the upper left show y pointing up and x pointing right. Near the top of the gap sits a circular mass labelled m, connected by a coil spring of constant k running horizontally to the right-hand wall. Near the bottom sits a circular mass labelled 2m, connected by a coil spring of constant 2k running horizontally to the left-hand wall. The two masses are joined to each other by a vertical elastic band of length L under tension T = 2kL, drawn as a double-headed vertical arrow between them. Each mass carries a small horizontal arrow marking its displacement coordinate: x₂ for the upper mass m, x₁ for the lower mass 2m. Both masses move only in the x direction, so the coupling band tilts slightly when they are displaced.]

(a) Write down the coupled differential equations describing the displacement of the masses from equilibrium {x₁, x₂}.
(b) Find the normal mode frequencies of the system.
(c) On the two figures included on the next page sketch the normal modes of the system; be sure to clearly indicate both the magnitude and direction of the motion of the masses.


Problem 3.3 (16 pts)

(a) An optical fiber consists of a solid rod of material with index of refraction n_f surrounded by a cylindrical shell of material with index n_c. Find the largest angle θ so that a wave incident on the solid rod from air with index n_a remains in the solid rod (express your answer in terms of n_f, n_c, and n_a).

[Figure 3: An optical fiber — a horizontal three-layer slab drawn in cross section. The middle layer, the core, is labelled n_f. Above and below it are cladding layers, both labelled n_c. To the left of the fiber is air, labelled n_a. A ray arrives from the upper left and strikes the flat left end face of the core, making an angle θ with the horizontal fiber axis; θ is marked between the incoming ray and the axis at the entrance face.]

(b) Unpolarized light propagating in vacuum reflects off the surface of a liquid with index n. The reflected ray strikes a screen 25 cm away at a height of 20 cm and is observed to be 100% polarized. What is n?

(c) Consider a medium in which waves propagate with a dispersion relation

    ω² = ω₀² + A²k²

where ω is the wave (angular) frequency, k is the wave number, and ω₀ and A are real constants.

    (i) What is the range of frequencies ω for which waves can propagate?
    (ii) Compute v_phase and v_group. Make a carefully labeled sketch of each as a function of ω in the plots provided.

[Figure 4: Plot the phase/group velocity — two empty grid plots side by side, provided for the student's sketches. The left plot has vertical axis labelled V_p (phase velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω; the right plot has vertical axis labelled V_g (group velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω. Both are blank graph paper with no data drawn and no numerical scale.]


Problem 3.4 (16 pts)

A monochromatic beam is incident on N slits, which results in an intensity pattern as a function of angle on a screen some distance away as shown in the figure below. Each slit has a width D and the distance between the centers of the slits is d. The distance between the screen and the slits is very large.

[Figure 5: Interference pattern due to N slits — a plot of Intensity (vertical axis, no numerical scale) against sin θ (horizontal axis, no numerical scale). The pattern is symmetric about the center. A tall central principal maximum sits at the middle, flanked by principal maxima of decreasing height on each side: the first-order pair is somewhat shorter than the central one, the second-order pair shorter still, and a small third-order pair is visible farther out. The fourth-order principal maximum is absent — the pattern is flat where it would fall, because the first diffraction minimum suppresses it — and small low bumps resume beyond that point. Between each pair of adjacent principal maxima there are three small subsidiary bumps.]

From the pattern deduce the following:

(a) The number of slits N on which the beam is incident. Explain your reasoning.
(b) The ratio d/D. Explain your reasoning.
(c) Now suppose that the width of the slits is reduced to ~0, while the intensity of the monochromatic beam is increased so that the intensity of the central maximum is unchanged. On top of the plot (showing the original intensity pattern in dashed lines) provided, draw the resulting intensity pattern.

[Figure 6: Plot the resulting intensity pattern as D → 0 — an empty plot frame provided for the student's answer, with the original intensity pattern of Figure 5 reproduced in dashed lines underneath.]


Problem 3.5 (20 pts)

A string of length 2L with mass density µ is placed under tension T and is fixed at both ends. At time t = 0, the displacement of the string is zero everywhere but it is struck so that a transverse velocity is imparted to a section of the string. The initial conditions of the string are (a ≪ L):

    y(x, t = 0) = 0

    ẏ(x, t = 0) = v₀      for L − a ≤ x < L
                = −v₀     for L ≤ x < L + a
                = 0       elsewhere

[Figure 7: The initial transverse velocity of the string at time t = 0; the initial displacement is zero everywhere — a horizontal string stretched between two hatched walls, the left wall at x = 0 and the right wall at x = 2L, with the midpoint x = L marked; the distance from each wall to the midpoint is labelled L. The velocity profile is drawn as a pair of adjacent rectangular pulses straddling the midpoint. Just to the left of x = L a rectangle of width a rises above the string to a height labelled v₀. Immediately to the right of x = L a rectangle of the same width a drops below the string to a depth labelled v₀ (i.e. −v₀). The velocity is zero everywhere else along the string.]

(a) Using the plot (Figure 8) provided, sketch the first three normal modes of vibration for this string, regardless of whether or not they are excited.

[Figure 8: Plot the first three normal modes — three identical empty plots stacked vertically, labelled (1), (2), and (3). Each shows a straight horizontal string at rest spanning the gap between a left and a right hatched wall, provided for the student to draw the mode shapes on.]

(b) What is the amplitude of the n-th normal mode after the string is struck? What is the lowest unexcited mode?

(c) Sketch the displacement of the string at time t = (L/2)√(µ/T) in the plot provided.

[Figure 9: Plot the displacement of the string — a single empty plot showing the straight horizontal string at rest between the left and right hatched walls, provided for the student's sketch.]


Problem 3.6 (18 pts)

A charged particle of mass M and charge +Q is attached to the end of a spring of spring constant k. The spring lies along the x-axis and the equilibrium point is at the origin. The particle is displaced from equilibrium by a distance A in the x direction, and released at t = 0. Assume that the size of the particle is much smaller than A, so it can be treated as a point charge, and that the damping rate is very small.

[Figure 10: An oscillating charge — a vertical wall on the left with a horizontal coil spring of constant k attached to it, extending to the right. At the free end of the spring is a circular particle labelled Q,M. Axes are drawn above the spring: z points up and x points to the right, with the origin at the particle's equilibrium position. The particle oscillates along the x-axis.]

(a) Calculate the electric field radiated by the particle along an arbitrary direction in the x−z plane, at a distance R, where R ≫ A.
(b) Calculate the total time averaged power radiated by the particle.
(c) Assuming that the power radiated does not change appreciably as a function of time, give a simple rough estimate of the time it will take for the particle to decrease its amplitude of oscillation to 1/e of its initial value. Is this assumption realistic?
(d) A more refined estimate can be obtained using that dA/dt = (dA/dE) × (dE/dt), and using the average power radiated over a given cycle for dE/dt. Use this to calculate the time it will take the particle to decrease its oscillation amplitude to 1/e of its initial value.

exchanges.student: hi, i’m working on this practice final rn and i’m kinda stuck on the waveguide problem 3.1 😅 can we start with part (a), like how to apply the boundary conditions to get \(k_y\) and \(\phi_y\)?
exchanges.tutor:
Hi! Let's think this through together. 😊

First — what's the physical boundary condition for an electric field at the surface of a perfect conductor? Specifically, what must be true about the component of $\vec E$ that's *parallel* to the conducting surface, right at that surface?

Once you tell me that, think about which walls of the waveguide are perpendicular to $y$ (i.e., located at some fixed $y$ value), since that's the direction your cosine depends on.

This is a direct request for solution guidance/methodology, not a stated answer, so there's no correctness to evaluate yet. It's also a conceptual/procedural question tied directly to the material."}

exchanges.student: i think the tangential electric field has to be 0 at a perfect conductor surface, right? so since \(E\) is in the \(\hat z\) direction, at the walls with fixed \(y\) that \(E_z\) has to vanish.
exchanges.tutor:
Exactly right! 🎯 $E_z$ is tangential to the walls at $y=0$ and $y=a$ (or wherever those walls sit — check your figure for which coordinate spans that direction), so it must vanish there.

Now look at your field:
$$E_z = E_0 \cos(k_y y + \varphi_y)\cos(k_x x - \omega t)$$

Apply the condition at the *first* wall, say $y=0$. What does $\cos(k_y \cdot 0 + \varphi_y) = 0$ tell you about $\varphi_y$?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STATE", "A_CURIOSITY"], "assessment_selection": "f,l", "assessment_justification": "The student is correctly stating the boundary condition principle (tangential E must vanish at a perfect conductor surface) and applying it correctly to conclude E_z must vanish at the y-boundaries, which matches the reasoning in the solution's part (a). This is a conceptual check/question phrased as a statement seeking confirmation, related to the material of the problem."}

exchanges.student: so that gives \(\cos(\phi_y)=0\), so i think \(\phi_y=\pi/2\) or odd multiples of it. is that the right branch to use?
exchanges.tutor:
Exactly — $\varphi_y = \pm\pi/2$ (or any odd multiple, but those just flip an overall sign or relabel, so $\pm\pi/2$ captures the physics). 👍

Now use that in your expression: with $\varphi_y = \pi/2$, what does $\cos(k_y y + \pi/2)$ simplify to (think of a trig identity)?

Then apply the *second* boundary condition, at the other wall, to pin down $k_y$. Which coordinate value marks that second wall — and what equation do you get from requiring $E_z=0$ there?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "f,g", "assessment_justification": "The student correctly derived that cos(phi_y)=0 leads to phi_y = pi/2 (or odd multiples), matching the boundary condition analysis for part (a). This is a correct intermediate result, and the student is explicitly asking for confirmation/guidance on whether this is the correct branch to proceed with, which is a question about how to proceed with the solution."}

exchanges.student: i think \(\cos(k_y y+\pi/2)=-\sin(k_y y)\), so at the other wall \(y=a\) i’d get \(\sin(k_y a)=0\). then does that mean \(k_y a=n\pi\), so \(k_y=n\pi/a\)?
exchanges.tutor:
Exactly! 🎯 That's exactly the reasoning — $\varphi_y=\pi/2$ turns the cosine into (up to an overall sign, which doesn't matter physically) a sine, and requiring $\sin(k_y a)=0$ at the second wall forces $k_y = n\pi/a$ for positive integer $n$.

So you've got both pieces:
$$\varphi_y = \pm\pi/2, \qquad k_y = \frac{n\pi}{a}$$

Nice work — that's part (a) done. Ready to move to part (b), the dispersion relation? What equation would you start from to relate $\omega$ and $k_x$ for a wave satisfying Maxwell's equations in vacuum/perfect dielectric inside the guide?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "f", "assessment_justification": "The student is deriving the boundary condition themselves, correctly computing cos(k_y y+π/2) = -sin(k_y y), and correctly applying the boundary condition at y=a to get k_y = nπ/a. This matches the correct answer (the tutor note indicates k_y=nπ/a is indeed correct, with the boundary at y=a rather than y=b as the printed solution has a typo). The student is asking for confirmation of their reasoning, which is correct, and it directly follows from working through the previous step, so this counts as correctly answering/verifying a derivation step."}

exchanges.student: i’m guessing the wave equation, so maybe \(k_x^2+k_y^2=\omega^2/c^2\)? i’m not totally sure if that’s the full dispersion relation here tho.
exchanges.tutor:
That's exactly it! ✅ Plugging your field into the wave equation
$$\nabla^2 \vec E - \frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 \vec E}{\partial t^2}=0$$
gives precisely $k_x^2 + k_y^2 = \omega^2/c^2$, and since you already found $k_y = n\pi/a$, you can substitute that in to write the dispersion relation purely in terms of $\omega$, $k_x$, $a$, and $n$.

Can you write that final form out? And once you have it, think about part (c): for a wave to actually *propagate* down the guide (rather than decay), what does $k_x$ need to be (real or imaginary)? What constraint on $\omega$ follows from that?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_HINT", "S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "d,f,g", "assessment_justification": "The student proposes a guess for the dispersion relation (k_x^2 + k_y^2 = ω^2/c^2), which matches the correct relation once k_y is substituted with nπ/a. This is a correct answer to what would be the tutor's likely prior question about the dispersion relation for the waveguide mode, but the student expresses uncertainty and doesn't fully commit or complete the substitution, making it somewhat tentative/incomplete. The student is also implicitly asking if their guess is correct, seeking confirmation, which relates to solving the problem."}

exchanges.student: ok so i think \(k_x^2=\omega^2/c^2-(n\pi/a)^2\). for propagation \(k_x\) has to be real, so \(\omega \ge n\pi c/a\), and the cutoff/lowest propagating freq for this mode is \( \omega_c=n\pi c/a\) i think?
exchanges.tutor: Great — that's exactly the right structure! Now think about which value of $n$ you should use to get the *lowest possible* cutoff frequency for this mode overall. Since $n$ can be $1, 2, 3, \dots$, which choice minimizes $\omega_c = n\pi c/a$?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_HINT", "S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "d", "assessment_justification": "The student derived the dispersion relation correctly and correctly identified the condition for real k_x, but incorrectly gave the general cutoff frequency as ω_c = nπc/a instead of recognizing that the lowest propagating frequency for this mode corresponds to n=1, i.e., ω_c = πc/a. This is an incomplete/imprecise answer to part (c) since it leaves n general rather than specifying the lowest frequency case."}

exchanges.student: that should be \(n=1\), so the lowest is \(\omega_c=\pi c/a\) (and \(f_c=c/2a\) if they want regular freq). i’m still a bit shaky on part (d) tho, esp getting \( \vec B \).
exchanges.tutor:
Nicely done on (b) and (c)! 👏

For part (d), you need $\vec B$ from $\vec E$ via Faraday's law:
$$\nabla \times \vec E = -\frac{\partial \vec B}{\partial t}$$

Since your $\vec E$ only has a $z$-component, $E_z(x,y,t)$, let's set up the curl. Do you remember how to compute $\nabla \times \vec E$ when $\vec E = (0,0,E_z(x,y,t))$? What are the $x$- and $y$-components of that curl in terms of partial derivatives of $E_z$?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "f,g", "assessment_justification": "The student correctly identifies n=1 gives the lowest cutoff frequency with the correct expressions for angular and regular frequency, answering the tutor's implicit check correctly (f). They also explicitly state uncertainty about part (d), asking for help deriving B, which is a request for guidance on how to solve that part (g). This isn't asking for a specific formula/theorem unrelated to the direct answer, nor is it off-topic."}

exchanges.student: i think \(\nabla\times \vec E=(\partial E_z/\partial y)\hat x-(\partial E_z/\partial x)\hat y\). i always mess up signs tho, so can u check that?
exchanges.tutor:
Let's verify carefully using the determinant formula:

$$\nabla\times\vec E = \begin{vmatrix}\hat x&\hat y&\hat z\\ \partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\ 0&0&E_z\end{vmatrix}$$

Expanding along the top row: the $\hat x$ component comes from crossing out the first row/column, giving $\partial_y E_z - \partial_z(0)$. The $\hat y$ component comes with a **minus sign** in front (cofactor expansion), giving $-(\partial_x E_z - \partial_z(0))$. The $\hat z$ component is $\partial_x(0)-\partial_y(0)=0$.

So what do you get for the $\hat y$ component — does it match what you wrote, or is there a sign difference?
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "f,g", "assessment_justification": "The student is presenting their own computation of the curl and explicitly asking the tutor to verify the sign convention/correctness of their expression, indicating uncertainty about algebraic sign errors. This is a request for confirmation/checking rather than a general conceptual question, and it directly pertains to solving part (d) of Problem 3.1. The expression itself is actually correct, so no error is present, but the student is asking for verification."}

exchanges.student: yeah ok, it matches what i wrote: \((\nabla\times E)_y=-\partial E_z/\partial x\). now i’m not sure how to integrate in time without messing up the cosine/sine part.
exchanges.tutor:
Good, so your curl is confirmed correct. Now let's compute those partial derivatives explicitly. You have

$$E_z(x,y,t) = E_0 \sin(k_y y)\cos(k_x x - \omega t)$$

Let's do the $x$-derivative first, since that's the one giving you trouble. What do you get for $\partial E_z/\partial x$? (Just apply the chain rule to the cosine — what's the derivative of $\cos(k_x x - \omega t)$ with respect to $x$?)

Once you have that, you'll set it equal to $-\partial B_y/\partial t$, and you'll need to **integrate over time** to get $B_y$ itself. Do you know a quick rule for "if $\partial B/\partial t = (\text{stuff})\sin(k_x x - \omega t)$, what is $B$?" — think about what function of $t$, when differentiated, gives you back a sine with that same argument.
exchanges.pedagogical_reasoning: {"intents": ["S_STRATEGY"], "assessment_selection": "f,g", "assessment_justification": "The student confirms their curl expression matches (correctly answering the tutor's previous question), and then asks for guidance on how to proceed with integrating the time-dependent term to get B from Faraday's law without making a sign/trig error. This is a request for help on how to proceed with the solution method, i.e., asking how to solve this step of the problem."}

exchanges.student: i think \(\partial E_z/\partial x=-E_0 k_x \sin(k_y y)\sin(k_xx-\omega t)\). then since \(-\partial B_y/\partial t=-\partial E_z/\partial x\), maybe \(\partial B_y/\partial t=-E_0k_x\sin(k_yy)\sin(...)\)? i'm getting lost in the minus signs again ngl.
exchanges.tutor:
Good — that derivative is correct: $\partial E_z/\partial x=-E_0 k_x\sin(k_y y)\sin(k_x x-\omega t)$.

So from $(\nabla\times\vec E)_y = -\partial E_z/\partial x = -\partial B_y/\partial t$, let's carefully track signs:

$$-\partial B_y/\partial t = -\big(-E_0k_x\sin(k_yy)\sin(k_xx-\omega t)\big) = E_0k_x\sin(k_yy)\sin(k_xx-\omega t)$$

So
$$\frac{\partial B_y}{\partial t} = -E_0 k_x \sin(k_y y)\sin(k_x x-\omega t)$$

Now for the integration step — forget the $y$-part and constants for a second, and focus on just this piece: if
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \sin(k_x x - \omega t)$$
what function $f(t)$ satisfies this? (Hint: try $f = C\cos(k_x x-\omega t)$ for some constant $C$, and differentiate it with respect to $t$ to see what $C$ needs to be.)

grade.judge_reasoning: Pedagogy (1.1-1.3): The tutor never gives away answers; every key result (φ_y, k_y, dispersion relation, cutoff frequency, curl formula) is elicited from the student through targeted questions. The student does the reasoning at each step. Scaffolding builds naturally from boundary conditions to dispersion to B-field. No meta-learning deductions are warranted as the tutor gives process-level guidance (e.g., 'think about what function of t, when differentiated, gives back a sine'). These constitute multi-paragraph monologues where shorter interactive prompts were more appropriate, triggering the 3.1.A.a deduction.
